title: Multiple spontaneous otoacoustic emissions as a single standing wave unstable to modulation
summary: Spontaneous otoacoustic emissions (SOAEs) have been interpreted either as cochlear standing waves or as local oscillations of hair cells. Multiple SOAE lines test both views, because each view must explain how the lines coexist. In the standing-wave view, each line is a separate resonance. In the intermodulation view, some lines are distortion products of others. Both explanations assume several independent oscillations. Independent oscillations, however, compete through the saturating cochlear amplifier, and the dominant oscillation suppresses the others. The saturation has another role besides suppression. The saturation also induces an oscillation of the gain at twice the frequency of the oscillation. In lasers, this oscillation of the gain, called the \textit{pump}, creates sidebands. This paper examines whether a cochlear standing wave can pump the gain by itself. A two-dimensional cochlear model with a step in the gain produced a single standing wave. The pump destabilized a pair of lines near the neighboring resonances. The other lines were phase-locked intermodulation products of the main line and the pair. A group of equally spaced SOAEs can thus arise from one self-sustained oscillation. The spacing follows the resonances of the standing wave, and the two explanations can hold together.

title: A passive, battery-free flexible metasurface for implantable millimetre-wave radar glucose sensing
summary: Continuous glucose monitors (CGM) break the skin barrier and require periodic sensor replacement. We investigated whether a passive, battery-free flexible metasurface, implanted beneath tissue and read by a commercial 60 GHz radar, can track blood glucose levels. The metasurface contained no electronics or reagents. We fitted a conical helix to the in-phase and quadrature radar signals across the frequency sweep and used its mean radius (the spiral radius) as the glucose-dependent feature. We tested glucose concentrations of 25 to 400 mg/dL in saline solution with and without the metasurface, and 196 to 596 mg/dL of total glucose in porcine whole blood beneath ex vivo porcine tissue and in a murine cadaver model with pulsatile blood flow. The metasurface was essential for achieving a monotonic sensor response; in saline, the coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of a logarithmic fit increased from 0.18 without the metasurface to 0.90 with it. In a murine (rat) cadaver model, the signal's spiral radius increased monotonically with glucose concentration despite pulsatile flow ($R^2$ = 0.91), and this monotonic behavior persisted through up to 6 mm of tissue. Although sensitivity decreased at higher glucose levels, each discrete concentration step remained clearly detectable. These results demonstrate that a shallow, passive implant paired with a commercial radar can effectively track blood glucose without requiring onboard electronics or batteries.

title: Mechanical acclimation of bacterial growth and division across generations
summary: Bacteria frequently encounter mechanical confinement in natural and engineered environments, yet how an abrupt change in mechanical conditions reorganizes growth and division across generations remains poorly understood. Using single-cell time-lapse microscopy, we tracked Escherichia coli across generations following transfer from liquid culture to glass-attached or glass-gel-confined conditions. This mechanical confinement causes an immediate reduction in elongation rate, followed by a multi-generational mechanical acclimation process whose dynamics depend systematically on confinement strength. During this relaxation, division behavior becomes more heterogeneous and cells temporarily depart from canonical adder-like size regulation, exhibiting timer-like correlation signatures. Using a stochastic cell-cycle model that resolves the generation-dependent correlation signatures of different size-control strategies, we show that changes in elongation rate alone cannot account for the observed transition in growth-division coordination. Despite this transient reorganization, the birth-size distribution remains bounded and largely preserves its shape throughout acclimation. Notably, adder-like regulation is restored before the elongation rate fully recovers, revealing distinct relaxation timescales for growth and size-control dynamics. These results establish bacterial size control under mechanical confinement as a dynamical nonequilibrium process in which growth and division can transiently reorganize while global size homeostasis is maintained.

title: Solute pulse compression and spreading in power-law fluid flow through a semipermeable tube
comment: Submitted to Journal of Fluid Mechanics. Currently under review
summary: We investigate Taylor-Aris dispersion and filtration-induced compression of a solute pulse transported by a power-law fluid through a slender, semipermeable, circular tube. The wall permits solvent filtration, modelled by Starling's law, while completely retaining the solute. Lubrication theory and multiple-scale homogenisation yield a one-dimensional macrotransport equation with spatially varying effective advection and dispersion coefficients. An evolution equation for the axial variance identifies the competing contributions of mean-flow deceleration, dispersive spreading, and wall-induced concentration redistribution. Filtration causes the mean axial velocity to decrease downstream, allowing compressive advection to overcome dispersive spreading. A local critical-width criterion distinguishes instantaneous pulse contraction from spreading. We evaluate the contraction threshold using the integral variance balance and compare the predictions with axisymmetric convection-diffusion simulations. As the relative contributions of compression and dispersion evolve, an initially contracting pulse may reach a minimum width and subsequently spread. Power-law rheology modifies both the hydraulic field and the Taylor dispersion contribution. Under the reference conditions investigated, shear thinning produces greater cumulative pulse narrowing than the Newtonian case: at dimensionless time T=100, the pulse width decreases from its initial value by approximately 31 percent for flow behaviour index n=0.4, compared with 26 percent for n=1. Substantial pulse narrowing can coexist with an outlet solvent flow rate that is only a small fraction of the inlet value.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
summary: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
summary: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $ρ= 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.

title: Scan-specific k-space interpolation using deep Koopman autoencoders
comment: Submitted to Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (MRM) as a Research Article 16 pages, 9 figures and 1 supplementary figure
summary:
Purpose: To develop a scan-specific, interpretable k-space interpolation technique for the reconstruction of accelerated MRI data.
  Methods: A deep Koopman autoencoder for nonlinear k-space interpolation was developed consisting of an encoder, a linear layer for interpolation and a decoder. The resulting network is implemented using mean square error loss function on k-space neighbourhoods derived from the autocalibration signals (ACS), combining a prediction loss and an autoencoding loss. The approach was compared to GRAPPA and RAKI in 281 retrospectively undersampled brain datasets, using quantitative reconstruction metrics. In a subset of 52 randomly selected images, a clinical reader study compared the proposed approach and RAKI in a forced choice scenario and using a five-point ordinal scoring, assessing sharpness, SNR, aliasing and overall image quality. Additionally, the effect of varying parameters such as the number of autocalibration signals, the contribution of the autoencoding loss, the kernel size, and the latent space dimension for the proposed technique was studied.
  Results: The proposed approach showed improved quantitative metrics compared to GRAPPA and RAKI. Visually, the method showed higher resilience to noise amplification and improved preservation of sharp details. In the clinical reader study, the proposed approach was preferred overall to RAKI and yielded higher scores than GRAPPA and RAKI. The proposed method showed robustness to parameter variations.
  Conclusion: Deep Learning based k-space interpolation can be achieved using a Koopman autoencoder for k-space neighbourhoods.
  Keywords: Parallel imaging, Koopman autoencoder, nonlinear mapping, k-space interpolation, deep learning reconstruction

title: HydróDex: gotta match 'em all!
summary: We present a comprehensive hydrodynamic classification of stationary fluid profiles in first-order phase transitions within the constant-sound-speed model, a physically motivated extension of the standard bag model that allows the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the bubble wall and evolving the profile in the surrounding plasma, we systematically identify and classify all the possible stationary solutions. The classification recovers all previously known direct and inverse detonation, deflagration, and hybrid solutions, while revealing a new class of stationary configurations, termed mixed hybrids, featuring rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+ > c_-$, the classification in terms of the wall velocity $ξ_w$ and the asymptotic strength parameter $α_N$ further exhibits degenerate regions in parameter space, where multiple distinct stationary profiles correspond to the same physical inputs $(ξ_w,α_N)$. This non-uniqueness arises as the parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We also compute the kinetic-energy budget and the associated acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed-hybrid solutions, despite their oppositely directed flows, introduce no additional spectral feature, and their spectra can be closely mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with very different fluid profiles. Finally, we release HydróDex, a public code that implements the complete hydrodynamic classification, fluid-profile construction, kinetic-energy budget, and gravitational-wave calculation.

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
comment: 45 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making (World Scientific)
summary: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

title: Deciphering multiple binding modes in large protein complexes via Enhanced Sampling and beta-VAE: the CYFIP1-eIF4E case
summary: Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) drives cap-dependent translation, regulated by 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) competing for its dorsal and lateral surfaces. CYFIP1, a scaffold protein, is both a WAVE Regulatory Complex component and a non-canonical 4E-BP repressing translation via a short helical motif, linked to autism spectrum disorders and cancer. Prior work modeled only this isolated motif as a peptide, leaving the full interface uncharacterized. Starting from this preliminary evidence, we modeled the full-length proteins as flexible partners: all-atom simulations fed a data-driven docking search (HADDOCK3), which guided funnel-restrained Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics of a coarse-grained Martini 3 representation. Ten replicas accumulated 100 $μ$s of enhanced sampling. Funnel-restraint variables efficiently sample binding and unbinding but are structurally degenerate: direct clustering of the raw trajectory collapses these poses into poorly resolved groups. We instead reweighted the biased trajectories onto a contact-based latent space built by benchmarking PCA against a beta-Variational Autoencoder, then clustered minima of the equilibrium free-energy surface: only intermediate regularization resolved distinct, homogeneous modes. Three such modes recur, engaging eIF4E's canonical dorsal site, its non-canonical lateral site, and both. We find that CYFIP1 also engages eIF4E through a second surface, the same that mediates its WAVE-complex dimerization, and a basic patch. Both plausibly explain residual binding previously reported after motif mutation. This suggests its translational and cytoskeletal roles compete for the same surface. Most contacts on eIF4E fall outside this dorsal/lateral interface. This heterogeneous, plastic ensemble offers a structural basis for mutagenesis and therapeutic peptide design.

title: Influence of transverse oscillatory shear on the viscous fingering instability
summary: Oscillatory shear can delay the onset of viscous fingering. In addition, uniaxial translational shear also breaks the symmetry of the resulting pattern so that the interface evolves differently depending on its direction of propagation relative to the shear axis. We observe a delayed fingering onset and reduced subsequent finger growth rate for all directions as shear speed or amplitude increases. However, shear widens fingers growing in the direction perpendicular to shear and elongates those in the parallel directions. After onset, neighboring fingers in the perpendicular directions can reconnect near their base when the shear amplitude exceeds approximately five times the excess linear finger wavelength at the onset. Concentration profiles reveal smoother azimuthal edges and overlapping structures behind the tips. These observations show that shear smears individual fingers and connects neighboring ones. This correlates lateral fingering interactions with radial propagation.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
comment: 22 pages, including 10 pages of supplementary material
summary: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.

title: CARVE: A glycan-specific framework for assessing protein-glycan binding-pose quality
summary: Protein-glycan interactions depend on the precise three-dimensional arrangement of carbohydrates at protein-binding interfaces, yet reliable assessment of predicted complex structures remains challenging. Existing evaluations commonly rely on fixed root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) thresholds, which do not fully account for the structural diversity and conformational flexibility of glycans. Here we developed CARVE, a glycan-specific framework for evaluating protein-glycan structure predictions. Through topology-aware glycan parsing, CARVE integrates orientation RMSD (oRMSD), interface-ring RMSD (irRMSD) and the fraction of native contacts (Fnat) to assess glycan scaffold geometry, interface-ring placement and native-contact recovery. These descriptors define four quality categories (CARVE-Level) with geometric thresholds that scale with the degree of polymerization (DP), and a continuous CARVE-Score, which reproduced those categories on 25,068 independently generated poses without recalibration (macro-F1 = 0.892). Pairing these measures with glycan-specific topological, chemical and geometric validity checks, we benchmarked nine prediction methods on CARVE-Bench, comprising 1,974 experimentally determined protein-glycan complexes. Among the top 25 predictions per target, HADDOCK3 achieved the highest Acceptable-level success rate (47.0%), whereas no method produced a high-quality, structurally valid pose for more than one in five. Collectively, CARVE provides a standardized basis for assessing protein-glycan structure prediction methods and guiding the development of more accurate docking and co-folding approaches.

title: Global saddle selection and exact absolute-instability boundaries for convection in porous media with throughflow
summary: In the Darcy-Prats problem, horizontal throughflow leaves the temporal onset of convection unchanged but raises the heating required for a localized disturbance to grow at a fixed point. The saddle equations give five candidates, but only the saddles reached by deformation of the Fourier contour contribute to the growth. For $Ra>π^2$, $Pe>0$ we prove that the same off-axis pair contributes throughout the domain: no Stokes transition can change its contribution. Its growth gives a unique analytic absolute threshold, first reached by the lowest vertical mode. Rescaling transfers the selection to Forchheimer drag, transverse rolls of a power-law fluid, anisotropic permeability, an open upper boundary and a vertical magnetic field. A shift of the same growth function accounts for interphase heat exchange in a model of metallic foam. At prescribed throughflow the threshold increases strictly with either resistance coefficient. In particular, a vertical magnetic field raises the absolute threshold at fixed Péclet number. Tabulated thresholds check the reduction. Algebraic elimination gives the boundary polynomial, and frequency recovery selects its physical branch. At the Darcy level the selected saddles trace an arc of the elliptic curve 11a3, a degeneration of a genus-two family at nonzero shifted levels. Series inversion on this arc gives an integer weak-throughflow series and an all-order strong-throughflow expansion. Rational certificates establish the exact convergence radii of both series on the selected sheets.

title: Few-Shot Open-Set Hyperspectral Pixel-Wise Classification with Spatial Aware Label Propagation
summary: Pixelwise classification of hyperspectral images (HSI) is a fundamental task in remote sensing, but its deployment in real-world applications is often limited by the scarcity of labeled data and the presence of unknown classes at inference time. In this work, we propose Few-shot Open-set hyperspectral recognition from Self-Supervised Learning training (FOSSeL), a unified framework for few-shot, open-set hyperspectral pixelwise classification that does not require supervised training. The proposed approach first leverages self-supervised learning to construct a discriminative feature space from unlabeled data. Then, given a small set of labeled seed pixels, class predictions are obtained through spatially-aware graph-based label propagation over superpixel representations, enabling the joint exploitation of spectral similarity and spatial consistency. To address the open-set scenario, we introduce simple yet effective strategies to identify pixels that do not belong to the known classes. We evaluate FOSSeL on three benchmark hyperspectral datasets under multiple few-shot settings. The results show that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior performance compared to fully supervised methods while maintaining robustness in the presence of unknown classes. These findings highlight the potential of combining self-supervised feature learning with graph-based inference for practical HSI analysis in low-annotation and open-world scenarios.

title: Sign-switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature of liquid jets by microscopic laser-induced cavitation
summary: Localized forcing of liquid jets can trigger Rayleigh-Plateau breakup at low perturbation amplitudes or explosive fragmentation at high amplitudes, while controlled bending in the intermediate regime has remained unexplored. We show that femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation, seeded at the interface of a 100 micrometre-diameter water jet, produces a selectable curvature in 0.4-1 mm long segments. Cavitation rupturing at the liquid-air interface drives fast outward jetting and induces a slower recoil on the opposite boundary, which evolves on the capillary-inertial timescale and results in curving of the liquid segment. The curvature is governed by three laser parameters. Off-axis laser illumination on the jet shifts the refractive caustics and redistributes energy deposition between the front and rear interfaces. The resulting recoil imbalance determines the curvature sign, with a straight configuration in the balanced case. Laser energy offers additional control over the recoil impulse via plasma defocusing and nonlinear absorption in the liquid jet, where the response is bounded by axisymmetric deformation at low energy and explosive vaporization at high energy. Repetition rate sets the spacing between successive cavitation events and hence the length of the bent segment. Curvature extends across the segment for lengths of 6-10 jet diameters; shorter segments undergo Rayleigh-Plateau breakup, whereas longer ones bend mainly near their retracting ends. Our results offer a platform for optofluidic control of switchable and tunable macroscopic curvature in flowing liquid jets.

title: BeST: Beta splatted tomography for direct reconstruction from coherent imaging measurements
summary: Conventional coherent X-ray tomography requires the phase of each projection to be reconstructed with high fidelity. However, individual reconstructed projections might be flawed, e.g. due to positioning errors, yielding inconsistent tomographic reconstructions. By directly coupling phase retrieval and tomography, consistency is enforced through a common object volume. But reconstructing a full volume demands substantial computational resources. To reduce this demand, we introduce Beta Splatted Tomography (BeST), which represents the common object volume using compactly supported beta primitives with closed-form analytical projections, enabling efficient reconstruction directly from coherent scattering images. This representation substantially reduces the number of optimizable parameters compared to a voxel grid. We demonstrate BeST on experimental datasets from hard X-ray near-field holography and far-field ptychography measurements. In both cases, the joint technique improves reconstruction quality compared to two-step methods.

title: Near-wall sedimentation of short cylinders at low Reynolds numbers: Translational and angular velocity models and experimental validation
summary: The sedimentation of short cylinders near rigid walls involves coupled translational and rotational motion, for which readily applicable kinematic descriptions remain limited. In this study, theoretical expressions for the translational and angular velocities were derived by combining slender-body theory, semi-empirical finite-aspect-ratio corrections, and hydrodynamic descriptions of fluid inertia and wall effects. The resulting expressions were assessed through time-resolved sedimentation experiments with rigid cylinders of mean aspect ratios $\barχ\approx3.8$--$5.8$ in a rectangular duct at particle Reynolds numbers of $Re_{\mathrm P}\approx O(10^{-1})$. The experiments revealed distinct near-wall trajectories, including non-contact glancing motion and contact-induced flipping. For glancing trajectories, the predicted translational and angular velocities reproduced the principal features of the measured kinematics, with good qualitative and, over substantial parts of the trajectories, quantitative agreement. The comparisons also identified different ranges of applicability for the investigated wall corrections and showed that wall-induced effects dominated the angular velocity under the conditions studied. The resulting, experimentally validated expressions provide readily applicable estimates of the instantaneous translational and angular velocities of short cylinders near rigid walls and a reference for investigating additional influences on their sedimentation dynamics, including lower Reynolds numbers and particle or wall elasticity.

title: D2ToF: One-Step Diffusion for Depth Super-Resolution from Lightweight Single-Photon LiDAR Waveforms
summary: Single-photon LiDAR (SPL) sensors offer exceptional temporal resolution and single-photon sensitivity for depth imaging. However, cost-effective SPL arrays typically suffer from extremely low spatial resolutions (e.g. $8\times 8$ pixels), limiting their real-world utility. In this paper, we propose a novel, one-step super-resolution framework, D2ToF, Distilled Diffusion for Time-of-Flight, that bridges the gap between high-fidelity generative modeling and real-time execution. Our approach uses an amortized variational distillation strategy that allows for a measurement-based data consistency term to be incorporated directly into the one-step training objective. This encourages that the synthesized high-resolution depth maps are consistent with the captured low-resolution Time-of-Flight (ToF) histograms. To overcome the severe ill-posedness of upsampling extremely degraded inputs, we introduce a multimodal guidance strategy. By leveraging a foundational monocular depth model to extract structural priors from a high-resolution reflectivity image, our network is guided by a rich triad of the ToF histogram, reflectivity map, and relative depth estimate. Experimental results outperform evaluated baselines, achieving $16\times$ spatial super-resolution (from $8\times 8 \times 100$ histograms to $128\times 128$ depth maps) at an accelerated inference speed of approximately $83$ milliseconds.

title: Flow structure, heat transport, and dissipation in vertical-field magnetoconvection at similar Reynolds numbers
summary: We employ direct numerical simulations to investigate the effect of a vertical magnetic field on the flow structures, heat transport, and dissipation rates in Rayleigh--Bénard convection of a low-Prandtl-number fluid ($\mathrm{Pr} = 0.025$) at an approximately fixed Reynolds number ($\mathrm{Re} \approx 880$), maintained by adjusting the Rayleigh number to compensate for the Lorentz force. As the Hartmann number increases, the flow becomes more anisotropic, which strengthens the positive convective heat fluxes relative to the negative ones and thereby raises the Nusselt number, accompanied by a thinning of the thermal boundary layers. The total viscous and thermal dissipation rates are dominated by the boundary layers, whereas the total magnetic dissipation rate is dominated by the bulk. With increasing Hartmann number, the boundary-layer fraction of the viscous and magnetic dissipation rates increases, whereas that of the thermal dissipation computed from the temperature fluctuations decreases, owing to the suppression of temperature fluctuations near the boundary layers. The dissipation rates deviate from log-normality and are well described by stretched exponential distributions, whose tails become more extended with increasing Hartmann number.

title: DecompJSCC: Joint Source-Channel Coding With Decoupled SNR and Rate Adaptation
comment: 5 pages,5 figures,1 table. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology
summary: Deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) for image transmission must adapt to changes in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and available transmission resources. However, some existing joint-adaptive methods condition the encoder on the requested rate, while others apply static masks after encoding. The former couples latent formation to the rate request, whereas the latter cannot adapt channel selection to image content. To address these limitations, we propose DecompJSCC, which decomposes joint adaptation into SNR-conditioned latent formation and post-encoding rate control within a single model. The encoder applies SNR-conditioned block attention residuals across all stages, aggregating intra-stage and cross-stage semantic representations. At the receiver, an adapter performs SNR-conditioned affine correction. We introduce a post-encoding rate-adaptive channel semantic budgeting (RCSB) module whose shared gate selects channels of the formed latent by image content, adjusts their gains, and keeps exactly the requested count. This keeps the encoder output independent of the rate request for a fixed image and SNR. Experimental results show that DecompJSCC outperforms SwinJSCC and SA-RA-JSCC in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) across a range of SNR and rate settings, by 0.64 and 1.00 dB over SwinJSCC and by 0.97 and 0.96 dB over SA-RA-JSCC on Kodak and CLIC2021, while using only 7.5% of SwinJSCC's Adaptive ModNet parameters.

title: Compressible gas flow through porous media under forced pressure and fluxes: compressibility number and pressure curvature
comment: 55 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: Gas compressibility induces a nonlinear relationship between boundary forcing and pressure evolution in porous media. This matters in operations and experiments where inlet pressure, volumetric flux or mass flux is controlled, as each forcing produces a distinct transient approach to steady state. We analyze this systematically for isothermal gas flow, using the porous medium equation (PME), nondimensionalized in terms of a Peclet-type number $Π$ that compares the time scales of gas flow and pressure diffusion and measures the steady flow compression. At steady state, increasing $Π$ leads to a boundary layer near the outlet, of width $\simΠ^{-1}$, where the velocity and flow expansion scale as $Π$ and $Π^2$, respectively. Since $Π$ fixes the steady compression for all three inlet conditions, their transients can be compared directly. We derive a semi-analytical perturbation series in $β=2Π/(1+2Π)<1$, valid for the three inlet conditions, which remains convergent at large $Π$. Numerical solutions for $10^{-2}\leqΠ\leq10^3$ show that the effective pressure-squared diffusivity plateaus at boundary-condition-dependent values for $Π\ll1$, and scales as $Π^{1/2}$ for $Π\gg1$, explained by the slowest eigenmode of the linearized PME about its steady state. To resolve local flow compression, we introduce the pressure curvature, $κ=\nabla^2 p$, and interpret its evolution through a nonlinear advection-diffusion-reaction equation. Curvature fields reveal localized compression pulses that migrate downstream and dissipate as the system relaxes, while curvature moments highlight a $Π$-dependent crossover from compression- to expansion-dominated transients. Applications to gas chromatography and underground hydrogen storage are illustrated.

title: Active flow control based on topological data analysis and a DMDc reduced-order model for drag reduction
summary: Controlling and reducing undesirable vortical structures in unsteady flows is a major issue in aerodynamics. This paper presents an active control methodology that combines topological data analysis (TDA) through persistence diagrams, a reduced-order model based on dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) and receding-horizon model predictive control (MPC). Vortices are detected and characterised by the persistence diagram of the absolute value of the vorticity, which makes it possible to define a target flow in which only the useful vortices are retained. This target flow is computed offline in the reduced space by gradient descent, the derivative of a persistence diagram being defined through a parametrisation of the space of diagrams. The control loop then reduces to a small-dimensional convex quadratic program, whose construction we detail and whose cost we compare with that of an approach that places the diagrams directly in the cost function. The approach is applied numerically to the flow around an oscillating aircraft wing for seven vibration frequencies, and yields a mean reduction of the drag coefficient while preserving the main vortices.

title: Potential Flow, Stress, and Straightness in Flow Matching: Euler Error on Gaussian-Mixture Targets
summary: In linear flow matching, coupling straightness measures conditional displacement variance. The conditional covariance gives a kinetic stress in the Jeans balance. The virial identity relates the mean trace of the covariance to a radial moment of acceleration. Euler error also depends on how the flow propagates acceleration. On constructed Gaussian-mixture targets, closed-form couplings with matched straightness yield different median Euler errors. Learned fields from fresh minibatch assignments also yield different Euler errors from their partners at matched estimated straightness. The leading Euler coefficient accounts for more of the error variation than straightness in these experiments. We relate the additive-noise characterization of isotropic Gaussian sources to potential flow. A gradient constraint reduces velocity error on the independent isotropic Gaussian example and increases it on two examples with rotational exact fields.

title: The effect of particle shape on sunlight exposure in a wind-driven free-surface flow
summary: We investigate how nonspherical marine particles, such as microplastics, phytoplankton, and ice, are exposed to sunlight near the water surface in wind-driven surface boundary layer conditions. We measure the depth and orientation of these particles in a laboratory wind-wave tank, then use this data to model how much sunlight the particles would be exposed to in an aquatic environment. In particular, we explore how their orientation affects their sunlight exposure in these conditions, since most studies to date do not account for orientation, turbulent shear flow, and wind-waves at the water surface. We find that in all cases, particles prefer certain orientations, and this causes the average sunlight exposure of the particles to be 5 to 40\% higher than would be expected if their orientations were random. Further, we find that the mean irradiance depends on the ratio of the particle mixing length $L_m$ to the light decay lengthscale $λ$, and the nature of this dependence differs between disks and rods. Disks experience disproportionately greater mean irradiance at smaller $L_m/λ$ due to the vertical variation in their orientations. These results have important implications for accurately estimating the sunlight exposure of particles in the surface boundary layer.
